about.title: Fairfield Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Fairfield sits where I-80 meets the working heart of Solano County, and many people here earn a living on their feet, behind a wheel, or on a job site. When something goes wrong at work, the first question is simple: who pays for this? Your employer's workers' compensation coverage normally answers that question no matter who was at fault. It covers treatment and part of your wages, not pain and suffering. That changes when someone other than your employer caused the harm. A driver who hit your work van on Air Base Parkway or North Texas Street, a subcontractor who left a hazard on a Travis Boulevard build, a property owner who ignored a broken stair, or a manufacturer whose machine failed can each be held responsible in a separate claim. Fairfield recorded 645 injury collisions in 2025, with 912 people hurt, and a crash while working often opens both a comp claim and a third-party claim. We can help you understand which path fits your situation.

items.title: We help you see past workers' comp
items.desc: Comp is usually the only claim you can bring against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or other driver can be pursued separately. We can tell you whether a third party is in the picture.

items.title: Deadlines stay on your radar
items.desc: You have 30 days to report an injury to your employer, and any third-party claim carries California's two-year filing window. Contacting us early keeps both clocks from running out on you.

items.title: Retaliation is not something you have to accept
items.desc: California law makes it illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If your hours were cut or your job disappeared after you got hurt, that is worth raising with us.

items.question: I was rear-ended on I-80 while driving a company truck through Fairfield. Do I only get workers' comp?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were on the job, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost pay through your employer. The other driver, though, is a third party, so you may also have a separate injury claim against them for losses comp does not address. We can review the police report and explain how the two claims work together.

items.question: What happens if I miss the 30-day window to tell my employer?
items.answer: Report it as soon as you can anyway, in writing if possible. A late report can complicate a comp claim, but it does not always end it, especially if your employer already knew about the injury. Any third-party claim runs on its own two-year deadline, which a late employer report does not shorten.

items.question: Does your service charge me anything?
items.answer: No. Our service is free. We handle injury claims on contingency, which means you pay no attorney fee unless there is a recovery in your case.
